entries.title: System helps humans predict when self-driving cars will make mistakes
entries.content:
Self-driving cars are often controlled by deep learning models that sometimes fail in unexpected situations. For instance, the car might inexplicably brake and block the path of an oncoming emergency vehicle. A human driver or passenger may need to react rapidly to prevent a collision.

To help humans better anticipate a vehicle’s mistakes, researchers from MIT and autonomous vehicle technology company [Motional](https://motional.com/) developed a new method that provides clear explanations of the underlying model’s decisions.

Usually, the internal reasoning process of a deep learning model is opaque and difficult to understand. But the new method, called the Concept-Wrapper Network (CW-Net), translates that reasoning process into concepts that faithfully describe the autonomous vehicle’s decisions without altering its driving performance.

CW-Net explains the decisions of machine learning-based planners using understandable concepts, like “approaching stopped vehicle” or “close to cyclist.” These explanations can correct misconceptions drivers and passengers have about vehicle behavior and improve their situational awareness.

In road tests on a private track, CW-Net explanations helped safety drivers more accurately predict vehicle behavior; a larger simulation study with nonexpert users yielded similar results. These experiments show how CW-Net can provide important feedback for engineers as they troubleshoot in-vehicle artificial intelligence systems. In the longer term, this technique could boost the safety and transparency of autonomous vehicles, while building appropriate trust in drivers and passengers.

“This work shows how explanations are supportive to the human’s mental model and understanding of the behavior of a system, and how it could be used in engineering and development to improve the technology,” says Julie Shah, an MIT professor of aeronautics and astronautics, director of the Interactive Robotics Group in the Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL), and co-senior author of the [paper on CW-Net](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-10950-5). “Unless we are building these technologies in a way that we can rely on and predict their behavior, then it is a shaky and unsafe foundation for their use.”

She is joined on the paper by lead author Eoin Kenny, a former MIT postdoc who is now a senior AI researcher at J.P. Morgan Chase; co-senior author Momchil Tomov, a staff research scientist at Motional; as well as Motional team members Akshay Dharmavaram, Sang Uk Lee, Tung Phan-Minh, Shreyas Rajesh, Yunqing Hu, and [Laura Major, president and CEO of Motional](https://motional.com/laura-major). The research [appears today in *Nature*](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-10950-5).

**Faithful explanations**

Machine-learning-based planners act as the “brain” of a self-driving car. These powerful deep-learning architectures process data from the vehicle’s cameras and lidar sensors, generate a high-level summary of the vehicle’s environment, decide what the car should do next, and output a trajectory for it to follow.

The planners are usually black-box models, which means their internal decision-making process is so complex it is difficult to understand. This can leave scientists and safety drivers in the dark about why an autonomous vehicle made an unexpected decision, like phantom braking.

The researchers designed CW-Net to explain a vehicle’s decisions using understandable concepts, while ensuring those explanations accurately reflect the true reasons behind its behavior.

“Especially in high-stakes settings like self-driving cars, it’s important that the explanations are not potentially misleading. Because CW-Net is causally faithful in how it makes decisions, that provides certain guarantees around the explanations,” Kenny says.

CW-Net is a “concept classifier,” an AI algorithm that has been trained to predict the high-level concepts that exist within input data. The researchers plug the CW-Net module into the middle of an autonomous vehicle’s existing machine-learning planner architecture.

It translates the model’s internal reasoning process into understandable concepts, like “approaching stopped vehicle” or “close to cyclist.” Then it forces the final piece of the planning model architecture to use those concepts when it decides what the vehicle should do next. In this way, CW-Net ensures the concepts faithfully explain the vehicle’s actions.

At the same time, CW-Net uses the concepts it classified to generate clear explanations that are output along with the vehicle trajectory, in real-time.

“Instead of just wondering why the car stopped, having real-time data provides feedback that lets you test the system during deployment. You could also give that data to an engineer to potentially improve the system,” Kenny says.

The researchers trained CW-Net to predict concepts using a dataset of 130 million examples of scenes from self-driving cars, with multiple labeled concepts in each scene. Using such a large, labeled dataset enables it to identify concepts accurately in a wide range of settings.

They also designed CW-Net to mimic the driving decisions of machine-learning-based planners, so the module would not negatively impact vehicle performance.

In the end, CW-Net generates accurate, understandable explanations without altering the original deep learning model.

**Improving situational awareness**

To test CW-Net, the researchers deployed the module on a real autonomous driving test vehicle (a Motional robotaxi) on a private track with a safety driver. They found that CW-Net helped the safety driver better predict how the vehicle would behave in surprising situations.

For instance, the vehicle consistently stopped when it approached a cyclist, and the safety driver assumed it did so because it detected that cyclist. But CW-Net explanations revealed that the model wasn’t properly configured to detect the cyclist and chose a trajectory that would have caused a collision. Instead, it stopped because its emergency braking procedure kicked in when it got too close.

Armed with this information about the model’s mistake, the safety driver could reduce speed or engage manual driving mode sooner in similar situations. This could also help engineers fix the model to avoid this failure in the future.

In larger online simulation studies using real driving situations captured on the roads of Las Vegas, the researchers saw similar results. CW-Net explanations significantly improved participants’ abilities to predict how an autonomous vehicle will behave.

In the future, the researchers could extend CW-Net so the module can cover more concepts and explore different training and design techniques that could boost performance and improve interpretability.

“Our study shows how crucial interpretability can be to these high-stakes environments, and how it should be on the mind of people as they are making AI in the future, for self-driving cars or other safety-critical environments,” Kenny says.

entries.title: fix(agents): serialize native compaction with session writers (#135441)
entries.content:
```
fix(agents): serialize native compaction with session writers (#135441)

## What Problem This Solves

Primary native compaction could start while the same OpenClaw session still owned an active writer. Codex treats manual compaction as a turn-like task and replaces an active task, so the overlap could interrupt the user turn and strand compaction before its terminal item.

## Why This Change Was Made

The host compaction coordinator now admits primary native harness and native CLI control operations through the existing per-session and global lanes. It revalidates the Codex session owner after admission. Direct compaction for callers that already own a lane remains unchanged.

The contributor's client-router wait, extra timeout, and duplicate rejection test were removed. A route can end before OpenClaw finishes its transcript checkpoint, so route lifetime was not the writer ownership boundary.

## User Impact

Codex-backed turns finish and persist before queued native compaction starts. The change does not add configuration, retries, timeouts, locks, or compaction policy.

## Evidence

- Current-main red at `0fafd993b4f93af51037dd9e29f69fcb94479a6e`: the compaction request preceded writer completion, Codex interrupted the writer, and the compaction item did not complete.
- Exact-head green at `64c0b970febf7dadb4814e10d24632e6e5d6ee92`: writer command completed, writer turn completed, compaction request started, and the context-compaction item completed in that order.
- Transcript proof: both unique markers remained after compaction, and a separate follow-up turn recalled them.
- Regression proof: the native CLI ownership test fails on pre-repair head `250755ad0768f80197b2d87d1690c6bc1703fbcb` because compaction starts after the writer claim changes; it passes on this head without starting native I/O.
- Focused tests: all 173 compaction owner tests passed.
- Focused lint, format, and `git diff --check` passed.

### Real runtime order

| Baseline | Exact head |
| --- | --- |
| writer start → command start → compaction request → writer interrupted → compaction item start | writer start → command start → command complete → writer complete → compaction request → compaction item start → compaction item complete |

### Redacted event trace

```text
baseline 0fafd993b4f93af51037dd9e29f69fcb94479a6e
01 writer_turn_started
02 writer_command_started
03 compaction_trigger
04 compaction_request firstTurnCompleted=false
05 writer_turn_completed status=interrupted
06 compaction_item_started
-- compaction_item_completed missing

exact head 64c0b970febf7dadb4814e10d24632e6e5d6ee92
01 writer_turn_started
02 writer_command_started
03 compaction_trigger
04 writer_command_completed
05 writer_turn_completed status=completed
06 compaction_request firstTurnCompleted=true
07 compaction_item_started
08 compaction_item_completed
```

Exact-head assertions: writer terminal `ok`; compaction `ok`; completion marker present; input and completion markers persisted; separate recall turn terminal `ok`; recall returned `WRITER_RECALL_OK`.

Co-authored-by: Ayaan Zaidi <hi@obviy.us>
```

entries.title: Your smartwatch may be overestimating calories burned by 25 percent
entries.content:
One of a [smartwatch](https://www.popsci.com/gear/looking-back-apple-watch-fashion-accessory/)’s main selling points can be its ability to track the calories burned while exercising. But similar to the [health tech industry](https://www.popsci.com/health/apple-forever-chemicals/)’s “[10,000 steps](https://thehill.com/homenews/nexstar_media_wire/4661381-10000-daily-steps-was-a-marketing-ploy-do-you-really-need-to-hit-it/)” selling point, new research strongly suggests a wearable’s workout assessment may overestimate your efforts—and in some cases, the readings are off by as much as 25 percent.

“You can’t treat the calories burned number it gives you as an accurate number, because it’s not,” Florida International University kinesiologist [Jason Kostrna](https://case.fiu.edu/about/directory/profiles/kostrna-jason.html) said during a [recent profile](https://news.fiu.edu/2026/your-smartwatch-is-lying-to-you-about-how-many-calories-you-burned-in-your-last-workout).

Kostrna and his colleagues compared four of the most popular fitness wearables on the market: the Apple Watch Series 8, Samsung Galaxy Watch 5, Fitbit Sense 2, and Garmin Forerunner 955 against clinical-grade measurement equipment. They then asked 58 adult volunteers to use a stationary bike during a controlled workout session, while alternating between moderate and intense activity. Their results were simultaneously recorded by one of the commercially available wearables, as well as a COSMED K5 metabolic analyzer. For reference, COSMED fitness equipment can be seen during James Bond’s physiology assessment scene in the 2012 film *Skyfall*.

According to results recently published in the journal [*PLOS One*](http://dx.doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0353261), smartwatch calorie overestimations ranged between 15 and 25 percent. Apple was the most comparatively accurate, while Garmin and Samsung offered the most generous results. Meanwhile, the researchers needed to discard Fitbit from their trial entirely because the device repeatedly glitched during experiments. In some instances the Fitbit recorded a single calorie burned during an entire workout, or even failed to generate any assessment.

To put the larger findings in perspective: if your wearable claims you burned 500 calories at the gym, that number may be much closer to 350 calories. This may not seem too serious, but the errors can easily add up over time.

“You could be hundreds of calories off each week and easily end up in a calorie surplus when you think you’re in a calorie deficit,” said Kostrna.

Tests also consistently indicated that smartwatches become less accurate for wearers with higher body fat percentages. The exact reason is still unclear, but Kostrna’s team suspects the issue may stem from how each device’s algorithms are calculated. This information is often highly guarded from public scrutiny by the tech companies themselves.

“When the companies are developing those algorithms, we don’t know where the test data is coming from,” Kostrna explained. ” That’s why I think it’s beneficial for the companies to see this type of data, so they can refine their products over time.”

However, this doesn’t mean the devices are completely useless. Their caloric measurements should just be taken as generous estimates. Researchers suggest treating a reading as a best case scenario after each workout, while people with higher body fat index may want to view the actual numbers even more conservatively. At the same time, the study’s authors warn against solutions like more aggressive dieting, since the body still requires healthy foods to recharge and improve. In any case, Kostrna stressed that calorie monitoring should only be one part of a person’s larger fitness goals.

“Focus on how you’re feeling, and use data to get a little better over time,” he suggested.

The post [Your smartwatch may be overestimating calories burned by 25 percent](https://www.popsci.com/health/smartwatch-calories-burned-overestimate/) appeared first on [Popular Science](https://www.popsci.com).

entries.title: 153 million stolen driver's license scans expose a growing ID problem
entries.content:
More than 150 million driver's license scans were up for purchase on the dark web, highlighting the risk you take every time you hand over your physical ID.  
  

![Smartphone screen displaying a digital drivers license with a stylized mountain goat illustration and the name Mark P, above an icon instructing the user to hold the phone near a reader](https://media.appleinsider.com/gallery/68808-144977-digital-xl.jpg)  
Digital IDs could potentially limit some data breaches, but not until adoption becomes near universal

  
Recently, a dark web platform known as Nexus claimed to be selling more than 153 million driver's license scans. In addition to the driver's licenses, there were more than 10 million ID cards, 3 million travel documents and international IDs, and over 579,000 medical cards.  
  
*KrebsOnSecurity* [was alerted](https://krebsonsecurity.com/2026/09/fbi-probes-service-selling-153m-drivers-licenses/) to the existence of the dark web site on August 31. Upon visiting the site, *KrebsOnSecurity* found the 153 million figure plausible; a blank search in Nexus returned 11.5 million pages of results, with 15 results per page.

entries.title: Toyohiro Akiyama, first Japanese citizen and journalist in space, dies at 84
entries.content:
The first Japanese citizen to launch into space, Toyohiro Akiyama was also the first commercially sponsored cosmonaut and the world's first journalist to file reports while on a spaceflight.

[Akiyama, 84, died last Wednesday](https://www.collectspace.com/news/news-090126a-toyohiro-akiyama-japanese-journalist-mir-obituary.html), August 26, of lower gastrointestinal bleeding, news agencies in Japan reported. A funeral was held with his close relatives in attendance.

As a correspondent for the Tokyo Broadcasting System (TBS), Akiyama was chosen out of his 162 fellow employees who applied to fly to space in celebration of the network's 40th anniversary. He trained at the Gagarin Cosmonaut Training Center in Star City, located outside of Moscow, and was assigned to the Soyuz TM-11 crew.

entries.title: The Army just used a 20-kilowatt laser to take out three drones
entries.content:
This week, the US Army used a high-energy multipurpose laser to [shoot down three drones](https://www.wired.com/story/the-us-must-stop-underestimating-drone-warfare/) near the US-Mexico border, which official reports claimed were “posing a physical threat to US military personnel and CBP partners,” referring to Customs and Border Patrol.

The operation took place between the night of August 25 and the early morning of August 26 in the vicinity of the Rio Grande Valley in Texas and was led by the Joint Task Force Southern Border (JTF-SB), which operates under US Northern Command. Authorities confirmed that, during the operation, agents used technology derived from the Army’s High-Energy Multipurpose Laser (AMP-HEL) system, a [military program](https://www.wired.com/story/laser-wars-us-military-laser-weapons/) focused on implementing high-energy lasers for new defense capabilities.

Available information suggests that this initiative began in September 2025, when AeroVironment, a company specializing in defense technology, delivered the first two functional prototypes of these laser-based weapons to the US Armed Forces. Two new, improved systems were delivered as [the program was expanded](https://www.avinc.com/2025/12/18/av-delivers-jltv-mounted-locust-laser-weapon-systems-to-u-s-army/) in December of the same year. According to the manufacturer, this particular platform, called the Locust Laser Weapon System, is designed to be mounted on military vehicles, as the Army has done with the versions it has received.

entries.title: Here's How AI Watermarks Work (and How to Properly Check for One)
entries.content:
Recently, Anthropic announced [that](https://www.theverge.com/tech/980416/google-gemini-ai-watermarks-removal "open in a new window") its Claude models will soon begin [marking its text output with invisible watermarks](https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-text-watermark "open in a new window"). At the same time, Google [revealed that its own visible Gemini watermark](https://www.theverge.com/tech/980416/google-gemini-ai-watermarks-removal "open in a new window") on generated images will now be optional. These are just two contradictory examples of the wildly varied methods of watermarking AI output. So, let’s break down how AI watermarks work, and how you can detect them even when they're "invisible."

## How does AI watermarking work?

The exact method for watermarking AI output will depend on the type of media being generated, but the principle is generally the same: The generated media is embedded with data that is undetectable (or occasionally detectable) to the human eye or ear, but which identifies it as AI-produced. Watermark-detecting tools can then be used to identify if something was made with AI, without guessing or using an [unreliable AI “detector”](https://lifehacker.com/why-you-shouldnt-trust-ai-detectors-1850369642). Here are some examples of how watermarks may be implemented for various media types.

* **For images:** Since the pixels of an image are mathematical values, they can be slightly modified to embed a digital signature, without perceptible changes to the image itself. Google’s [SynthID](https://deepmind.google/models/synthid/ "open in a new window"), for example, distributes an invisible signature across any generated image, so even a cropped version will still contain detectable portions of the watermark. Note: This is distinct from the visible gray symbol in the corner of Gemini images. Even if you turn off the visible Gemini watermark, the invisible one remains.
* **For audio:** Embedding a watermark in audio files can be even easier, placing signature sounds outside the range of human hearing (typically below 20Hz or above 20,000Hz). SynthID has an audio component that can be heard by watermark detectors, but remains imperceptible to the ear.
* **For video:** Naturally, generated video tends to use a combination of both of the above watermarking methods, though it’s worth keeping in mind that someone making fake content could, for example, generate AI audio to accompany real video, meaning the watermark might appear in one piece of the content, but not another.
* **For text:** Every next word an LLM generates comes with a probability score. The sentence “The cat is” could end with “fluffy,” “cute,” or “small.” Each one of those words is given a percentage likelihood that it will appear. Text watermarks work by inflating the chances that certain sets of random words will appear. This can make it possible to detect LLM-generated text without changing its semantic meaning. However, this tends to work better for longer pieces of text, which provides more chances to detect the presence of less-likely words.
* **For metadata:** While not strictly a watermark, C2PA is a framework for adding metadata that can help verify the origin of a piece of media. Some camera manufacturers, for example, have implemented C2PA to give photographers a traceable record of where an image came from. This can also include noting whether an image was generated with AI tools.

While SynthID originated with Google’s DeepMind, the company open-sourced the protocol, and now it’s also used by other AI companies, including OpenAI. Some companies. conversely, do not use a watermark at all—and among those that do, the implementation can be inconsistent between tools. In other words, the presence of an AI watermark can confirm something *was* made or modified with AI, but the absence of one can’t prove it *wasn’t*.

## How can you detect AI watermarks?

Despite SynthID and C2PA being relatively common, it’s still kind of a crapshoot to properly detect the presence of watermarks or metadata that will confirm if a piece of media was generated with AI. [OpenAI has a standalone tool](https://openai.com/research/verify/ "open in a new window") to check for SynthID or C2PA in a file, and Google lets you access its verification tools via Gemini or, with the right prompting, directly via Google itself.

However, these tools have limitations. OpenAI’s detector, for some reason, only seems to detect media generated by OpenAI itself. During my testing, I tried uploading images generated via Gemini—which could detect its own SynthID watermark—and OpenAI’s tool did not find it.

Meanwhile, Google created [a SynthID Detector portal](https://deepmind.google/models/synthid/ "open in a new window"), but it’s currently available on an invite-only basis, specifically for journalists and verification professionals. You can still access some SynthID detection functions via Gemini or Google, though in some cases, you’ll need the right prompts to do so. In my testing, when asking “is this real” for a known AI-generated image via Gemini, the tool invoked a verification tool to check for SynthID. However, when doing the same process via Google, the LLM’s output resembled a visual analysis instead. It only invoked a SynthID check when specifically asked to do so.

Even if you do your diligence to check for every version of a SynthID watermark or C2PA metadata, it’s still possible that a piece of media could have some other form of watermark that requires a different detector. Unfortunately, unless you have a strong indicator of which tool was used to create a piece of generated media, it can still be difficult to thoroughly check for every kind of watermark.

When it comes to text-based watermarks [like the kind Claude](https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-text-watermark "open in a new window") or even Gemini use, detecting them can still be very difficult. For starters, neither offers a public way to check for the text watermark just yet (Google's SynthID Detector portal can do so, but it's not generally available).

## Can AI watermarking be circumvented?

With enough work, any watermark can technically be removed, though [SynthID specifically is pretty resistant](https://arstechnica.com/ai/2026/07/tested-google-synthid-works-great-but-labeling-ai-content-may-be-a-losing-game/ "open in a new window") to most typical forms of modification. An AI-generated image with a SynthID watermark that has been cropped, filtered, or modified can still retain enough of its original watermark to be detectable. It’s not impossible to remove, but it’s generally hard to do so accidentally.

Removing metadata like C2PA, on the other hand, is considerably easier. For images, that’s as simple as taking a screenshot. A screenshot of an image essentially creates a new image file based on the pixels visible on the screen. This means that any watermark that affects those pixels can remain, but an entirely new set of metadata is created, wiping any C2PA data along with it.

That means that if you want to maintain a metadata chain that lets you prove the authenticity of an image, it’s important to download or upload the specific original files and make sure any editing tools you use support maintaining that metadata.

Text watermarks are among the easiest to get around. Since they work by simply altering the probability that certain words will appear, running text through another AI tool that rephrases the words without using a watermark, or even manually rewriting a block of text, can potentially remove the watermark.

## Does a watermark always mean a piece of media was AI-generated?

It’s important to keep in mind that a watermark can be *added* to an authentic piece of media. If someone uploads an authentic photo to a tool like Gemini to perform simple edits, the output image will have a SynthID watermark, too. This doesn’t mean the whole image is inauthentic, but it will still be flagged by watermark detectors.

Similarly, it’s possible to generate an image of a subject, cut the subject out, and add it to an image using traditional manipulation techniques like Photoshop to create an inauthentic image that’s mostly made from an authentic image. Whether or not the watermark will remain on the portion of an image that was AI-generated can only be determined on a case-by-case basis.

As mentioned before, the absence of a watermark cannot prove that an image is authentic. Even the presence of a watermark can’t prove that the substance of an image isn’t real. Watermarks and metadata are simply tools to help you figure out where a piece of media likely came from and how it might’ve been modified. Ultimately, it’s still up to you to [verify the things you see and hear online](https://lifehacker.com/the-fastest-ways-to-fact-check-a-viral-tweet-1848588918).

entries.title: Jeremiah Brown is building a post-Love Island creator career one book at a time
entries.content:
![Jeremiah Brown](https://helios-i.mashable.com/imagery/articles/01yqC66yScQRdGPPhlCbg2l/hero-image.jpg)

[Jeremiah Brown](https://mashable.com/life/jeremiah-brown-love-island-tiktok-booktok) didn't leave [*Love Island USA*](https://mashable.com/entertainment/love-island-usa-reveals-season-8-winners) with a master plan to become a [full-time creator](https://mashable.com/creator-hub-creators-content-creation-tools-instagram-tiktok). In fact, before entering the villa, his social media presence was relatively sparse: a few book reviews, some funny videos, and an Instagram account that functioned mostly as a modeling portfolio.

But when Brown returned to the real world, he quickly realized just how many people were paying attention. Rather than simply ride the post-reality-TV wave, he and his older sister sat down and created a seven-page strategy for what came next. The pillars were simple — books and mental health, fitness and travel, and the lifestyle content that already reflected his interests.

SEE ALSO:
[The Mashable 101: The creators defining the internet in 2026](https://mashable.com/life/top-creators-defining-2026-mashable-101)

That strategy has since turned Brown into something of an unexpected BookTok favorite. He runs a book club, hosts IRL reading meetups, streams on Twitch, and recently attended Kai Cenat's Streamer University, where he spent five days broadcasting what he calls the "unfiltered, unedited version of Jeremiah Brown."

Mashable spoke with Brown about turning reality-TV attention into a sustainable creator career, why comments matter more to him than views, embracing his reputation as a "performative male" who drinks matcha and reads, and the advice he'd give anyone trying to build an audience online.

![Jeremiah Brown](https://helios-i.mashable.com/imagery/articles/01yqC66yScQRdGPPhlCbg2l/images-1.fill.size_2000x877.v1788284043.jpg)

Jeremiah Brown is beating the performative male allegations one book at a time.
Credit: Ian Moore/Mashable/Getty Images/Entangled Publishing/HarperCollins/Twitch//Streamer University

**Mashable: You recently attended Kai Cenat's Streamer University. What was that experience like?**

**Jeremiah Brown:** One of one. I’m not gonna lie, it’s probably a top-five experience I've ever had in my life. It's just so unique in the way that, one, it’s a thing to get a bunch of content creators and streamers together because the energy is just palpable in every room you’re in. And two, everyone was so nice and welcoming.

Usually, I feel like, especially in LA, it can be very — not cliquey, but, you know, very transactional. But at Streamer University, everyone was in everyone's TikToks, everyone's livestreams, nothing but love. And the thing that really caught me off guard was the welcoming and acceptance of everyone's communities. Every TikTok I was in, every livestream I popped up in, and vice versa, it was like, "My two worlds are colliding. I have no one to tell about this." It was just such positive feedback from every community, which was really refreshing.

Because I'm not gonna lie, with *Love Island*, when you cross over, it can get very territorial, like, "Why is he there? He's clout chasing." But this was content creators coming together to make amazing content, and it was one of the best experiences of my life.

**What was the biggest lesson you took away from it?**

Don’t be scared to ask people. Because I had the benefit and the blessing of coming in with a little bit of a platform, so it was kind of easier for me to walk up to people and be like, "Let's do this, let's do that."

But it was a blessing just to learn from the smaller and the bigger content creators. If somebody had 100 viewers, I was popping in like, “Let's go get food." And then learning from Agent and Ludwig's classes, because I actually went to class most of the time. They had amazing classes. I learned a lot about actually creating content, whether it’s hooks or longevity.

**When I was tuning into some of the streams, it felt very much like a reality show. And you obviously have a reality show background. So was the transition from reality TV to streaming that big of a jump for you?**

No, honestly, that’s a beautiful question. Because I was on stream the other day**,** telling my chat the difference between reality TV and livestreaming. How do I say this in the nicest way possible? When you do a reality television show, you kind of give them your life. In the sense that, obviously, I'm very blessed to do it and all the nice things, but at the end of the day, whatever they want the world to see, they choose.

And so why I feel like Streamer University was so important for me is, you know, on reality shows, I haven’t always gotten the best edit. So being live for five days straight, it's really the unfiltered, unedited version of Jeremiah Brown that you get to learn and see, love or hate.

So it’s kind of like, this is who I actually am, not the edit I got however long ago. This is who I actually am as a person. Take it or leave it. This is me tired, angry, happy, joyous, exhausted, full of energy — every single emotion. We streamed like 120 hours in five days. So it was beautiful to just show the world, like, "This is who I am." This is not whatever narrative they want to say. This is who I am. This is my personality.

Walk with me, or you don't. Honestly, that was the biggest blessing because I got to show people who I am without any editors or storylines or narratives.

---

**Featured Video For You**

---

Jeremiah Brown is building a post-'Love Island' creator career one book at a time

---

**You mentioned spending time with a bunch of creators from different spectrums of the internet, which I think is the really cool part about Streamer University. Did it change the way that you thought about your own content at all?**

Yes and no, because I’m always gonna go back to things I love, like books, sports, fitness, mental health, things like that. But at the same time, it let me just enjoy whatever. Because I can’t dance, for example. I can’t dance, and this is very silly, but I was doing dancing TikToks with everyone just because if they’re posting it, it's OK, you know? And then I’ll just repost it.

So it was fun to get out of my comfort zone and be the goofier version of myself because I feel like it's not that I can't always show that in my content, but it was awesome to just pull up and livestream and be like, this is me when I don’t make sense, this is me when I do make sense, you know?

**Did you get much reading done while you were there?**

Yeah. I brought *Binding 13* and *Fourth Wing*. For *Fourth Wing*, I ran a challenge where I had content creators read a paragraph, and if they didn’t stutter or mess up, I’d gift them subs on Twitch.

And then, *Binding 13* was a book I was doing for my book club. I just finished it, actually, like, a week ago. I read that on the plane and on the bus, but not when I was streaming. It was wake up, stream, sleep. Wake up, stream. We never turned off.

**Did you meet anyone there who surprised you or inspired you?**

Honestly, low-key almost everyone. Because I was like, damn, there's this whole world. The world I'm in with content is usually fellow Islanders, like 80 percent of them. It’s just my fellow Islanders because they’re my friends. They’re my friends now.

And this, I got to meet the world of Benji, Crystal, Davis, Alyssa, Agent, and all the AMP guys again. So yeah, honestly, it was just crazy. I was like, everyone's so funny and so cool. And there was very, very little ego or, "I'm not gonna do this because you’re a brand-new streamer." I didn’t get a sense of that, at least. Even when they were around a small streamer and a bigger streamer, they would do segments together. So yeah, it was really just beautiful, honestly.

**What about from your roommate Davis? Did you learn anything from him?**

I met Davis randomly in San Antonio last year. He reached out, and I was in town for an appearance a year ago. And I got to meet Kai because of him, and Duke, and got back involved in streaming because of him.

And then a year later, I’m now his roommate. We got super close. That’s my bro now. We FaceTime, we play *Black Ops* together. Him, Alyssa, and I just did a 24-hour handcuff stream a couple of days ago. And so yeah, now we have a trio, and it's a thing on the internet. It's been a blessing.

**It seems like a lot of what you’ve done actually fits really well with what you're doing now as a content creator. Obviously, you started as a model, and I feel like modeling is all about getting comfortable in front of a camera, having people looking at you, and personal branding is really important as a model. You were on *Love Island USA,* and that, too, is about getting comfortable with people’s perceptions of you and with being watched by cameras. Do you feel like the things that you’ve done have better prepared you for this career?**

A thousand percent. Because, funny enough, I never wanted to be a content creator. I had like 10 videos up, I think, before I went on *Love Island*. Like five book reviews and three funny ones. And yeah, I posted on Instagram once a month to show people I was working as a model, more like a portfolio, because they’d always want to see your Instagram.

I've been a model since 2018. So that was seven years before *Love Island*. Always being in front of the camera prepared me for photo shoots and interviews.

And then just reading books too, like *How to Win Friends and Influence People*, books like that on how to just talk to people and genuinely form connections, so things are just easier to do. I think a thousand percent.

Because if you've never been in front of a camera and then all of a sudden you’re in front of 55, doing interviews every single day or appearances, obviously, there was still a lot I had to adapt to in terms of the face-to-face, taking pictures and stuff like that. But long story short, being a model for so long definitely helped.

**It's always interesting to watch the careers of the Islanders when they leave the villa, or really any major reality show, right? Because you get all of this attention, you get a huge boost across your socials, and your numbers are way up. Can you tell me what the first few weeks out of the villa were like when you had all of this attention on you? What was your thought process? Were you immediately like, "How do I turn this into something bigger?" Or were you just trying to get your bearings?**

A mix of both. Because there’s one side of it, like, I need to get grounded, I need to see my family, I need to talk to my therapist, I need to get back to my books.

And then the other side is like, OK, now that I do have this, because I didn't expect it. One, I didn't know the power of the show because I wasn’t too familiar with the world, and I wasn't on TikTok. And then two, I was only there for half the time. No final four, no couple. So I’m like, OK, I was there for a little bit, had my thing, and then I was like, people really resonate with me and my content or my previous content, my book reviews.

And so it was a mix. Like, OK, I’m gonna go get grounded. And then luckily, I have the best big sister in the world. I went to her crib and just made a brand pillar and really did all the steps, like a seven-page document on how to maximize and capitalize on this opportunity I’ve been given.

**Wow, shout-out to your big sister. What were some of the things that were in this document, if you don’t mind sharing?**

Basically, it was like, what am I? What do the next steps look like? What are my pillars? So books slash mental health, fitness slash travel, and then just overall lifestyle, family content, and mukbangs.

And it’s kind of like, OK, these are things that are not easy for me to do, but it’s what I genuinely love. So I won’t — obviously, you can get burnout — but if I’m doing something, if I talk about books, I’ll never shut up, you know? So it’s always something I can go back to that I’m passionate about. Or anime, for example.

It’s basically just the best way for me to produce content that doesn’t end in burnout, and it’s most genuine because I’ve read, you know, hundreds of books. So it’s just stuff like that.

**It sounds like books have really inspired you over the years. Obviously, they’re a huge foundation of your content. Do you remember the book that got you into reading?**

*The Invention of Hugo Cabret* is one of my favorites from, I think, middle school or high school. But honestly, it was my uncle’s comic book shop when I was a kid, in elementary school. We’d drive down to Portland, Oregon. I think it’s still there, but he doesn’t own it anymore. I read all the time from that.

And then, in middle or high school, there was AR reading. So you’d read and take quizzes to get pizza and candy. So that’s why I started it. And then I stopped because of college. Like, I’m not gonna read for school and for fun.

But then COVID hit, and the first book that really got me on my mental health journey was *Mindset* by Carol Dweck. And then I went to Ryan Holiday and Stoicism. I think Ryan Holiday and his Stoicism books, like *Ego Is the Enemy*, *The Obstacle Is the Way*, and *Stillness Is the Key*, really made that shift where I just dove into all things self-mastery. And I was like, how do I become the best version of myself?

**Backing up a little bit, when you would read comic books in your uncle’s store, were you a DC guy or a Marvel guy? I just need to know.**

Punisher was my favorite, so Marvel. But I loved them all. Punisher was my favorite graphic for sure.

**Got it. OK. I’m a DC girl, so it’s OK.**

DC’s fire. And like *Ponyo*, *Totoro* — he put me onto all that. Yeah, he’s the best.

**I love that for you. Love the Ghibli journey. So you established reading and mental health as pillars. Where did you go from there? How did you go from making this document to actually executing on it?**

It was really just what works and the feedback. People would come up to me at the airport, anywhere I’d go, and say, "I love your book reviews." And I’m like, that has to mean something. So then I started a book club, and that’s been doing really well. People are part of that.

So it’s really a mix of what’s working and a mix of what I love to do. Because at the end of the day, I have to post it for myself. Because if I only post for other people, that’s how you get burnout and start chasing trends. Although I do the trends. I can’t say I’m not a trend guy. I do all the trends too.

So it’s really just branching out to whatever is popular at the time — the Finals, the World Cup — and then always coming back to what people know me as and what I love to produce. So I’ll do a bunch of sports videos, a mukbang, and then boom, here’s a book review. Just things like that.

Really, the execution was just making sure I’m staying true to my values and who I am, and then trying to show that through my content.

**As we said, when you leave a reality show, you get a lot of eyes on you, a lot of attention. But for some Islanders, some reality TV stars, it fades pretty fast, right? They have a finite window to capitalize on. But with you, it has seemed to really stick. Do you feel like that intentionality is what separates you from some of the others?**

Yes and no. I remember the first six months out of the villa, every day I thought, "When is this gonna stop? When is this gonna stop?" I was scared all the time. But then Jalen Brown from the show just said, "One day at a time." So I just try to live by that.

In the sense where it’s like, I'm just gonna keep doing — obviously I'm gonna evolve and do better content. I’m doing a produced book series now, a book review series, things like that. So I’m gonna keep evolving my content.

But yeah, at the end of the day, you kind of just find ways to keep going because short-form is amazing, but you have to build a brand in the sense of, why would people still watch, whether it’s streaming or long-form or hosting or a TV show again?

But yeah, to answer your question, I have no idea. TikTok can get banned. You really just don’t know. So I kind of just enjoy it every day and make content I love to make.

> [View this post on Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DcMiaW5SglP/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)
>
> [A post shared by Jeremiah Brown (@findjeremiah)](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DcMiaW5SglP/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)

**Your new series, Matcha to Read...I love the title. But I do have to say, men who drink matcha and read in public are often called performative males. So how do you feel about that?**

It's hilarious because I filmed my first *Matcha to Read* before Streamer University, and I posted it after because they were editing it. And all my new supporters — or some of them are trolling, of course — were like, "Performative king," blah, blah, blah.

And it’s like, OK, I get it. I feel like, as a male, especially a young Black man, people aren’t known for going on reality TV and then popping out with, "By the way, guys, I love books, anime, mental health." They’re kind of like, well, most people do fitness, which there’s nothing wrong with. I'm saying usually it’s like *Love Island* and fitness, which is awesome. I work out, of course, it’s just not my main type of content.

And so I say that to say I get the comments, but it’s like, if you look at my history, I've had matcha videos. I have three sisters, so I’ve been put onto matcha my whole life. I’ve tried all the Frappuccinos. I remember there’s a video where my sister made me say "pinkity drinkity" as a prank on her phone when we went to get coffee.

So I've tried all the matchas for years and years and have read all the books since I was a kid. And so I can only laugh. But the reason why I can laugh is that I have a digital footprint where there’s proof. If I didn’t have proof, I’d be like, “Oh my God, no guys, I promise.” But it’s like, I’ve been doing it, so it’s OK.

**You're like, "I'm about that life."**

Yeah. People have even seen my crib and are like, "You actually read?" I’m like, "Yeah." People ask in chat all the time, "You actually read?" Like, yes, bro. Yeah. People don't get the power of books. People don't get it.

**They really don’t. There’s an entire subreddit dedicated to women, or people, who will take photos of the person they’re dating’s bookshelves and post them on the subreddit and be like, “OK, should I be concerned?” Or, “What are your thoughts about my date’s bookshelf?” So if people saw your bookshelf, what do you think they would think?**

Honestly, they’d love it because I have ACOTAR, *Fourth Wing*, *The Housemaid*, I have all the popular books, and then I have all the self-mastery books. So I have every single category. I have *Circe*, *The Song of Achilles*. I have all the classics. *The Great Gatsby*. Like, yeah, everything.

**I’m really happy that you read *The Song of Achilles* for your book club.**

Yeah, that was the first one. It was the first one. It was beautiful.

**How do you decide what you’re gonna read for content versus what you’re gonna read just for yourself?**

Great question. I used to be able to do two books at once, but sometimes the schedule can get tough. At the beginning of the book club, it was a bit themed. So we did fantasy first, then a horror one for October, and then POC for February. And the last few months, like, I read *Fourth Wing,* and I just had them vote. So now I just — and then for classics we did a list of classics, and in my reading room they’d vote. So, the last six months, it’s really just been a voting system.

Once I read *Fourth Wing*, I was like, OK, you guys aren’t steering me wrong. And then I read *Binding 13,* and I was like, OK, I'm gonna trust you guys because there’s literally like a one-percent chance I would have ever read any of these books without my book club. It would have been straight self-mastery.

"
People have even seen my crib and are like, 'You actually read?' I’m like, 'Yeah.' People ask in chat all the time, 'You actually read?' Like, yes, bro. Yeah. People don't get the power of books. People don't get it.
"

So even though it's for content, I fall in love with the books. *Binding 13*, bro, it made me cry probably like six times. It’s such a powerful book. And then now we’re reading *Keeping 13*. And then I have a book called *A New Earth* by Eckhart Tolle.

I'll read that when I can, but I'm gonna focus on *Keeping 13* because, one, I need to finish it for my book club, and two, it’s like a 600-page book. So yeah, I try to balance reading the main one first and, if I have extra time, going to the personal book.

**Got it. That makes sense. Because how do you read *Fourth Wing* and then not immediately go to the next book?**

I started *Iron Flame*. I forgot, yeah, I went from *Fourth Wing* to ACOTAR, which is kind of — actually, I should've done it the other way because *Fourth Wing* was popping off immediately. People are getting thrown off the parapet immediately.

And then ACOTAR was so slow. It was a good book, but the first one is so slow because it’s a buildup for the second one. I get that. People were telling me, “Yo, give it time.” But then I’m like 150 pages into *Iron Flame*, or 200, but I just kept having to stop to read ACOTAR. So it’s a balance to be had.

**Yeah, that first ACOTAR book, when you read the whole series, you’re like, OK, that’s actually maybe the slowest of the books. You’ve also hosted IRL book club meet-and-greets, which I love. What has it been like to see your fans or followers in person and interact with them?**

It was crazy. We did a pop-up one in Seattle, maybe in May. It had to be in May, yeah. And I had less than 24 hours to promote it, and I think we had like 70 people there.

So it was really sick just to talk about books with people who support me. We just yapped and someone brought me a matcha, ironically enough. And yeah, it’s just beautiful to see the power of books.

Because I was not on TikTok, I had no idea about BookTok or anything. I had no idea people still read or loved books. And then all of a sudden, I’m posting about it, and there are 500 comments saying, “This is my Roman Empire series,” and I’m like, I didn’t even know what that meant. I had to Google what “Roman Empire series” meant.

So it’s honestly just been a beautiful thing that they welcomed me into the BookTok space.

**We are in a bit of a reading crisis, so to have somebody like you really promote books and reading is wonderful. But at what point did you decide, OK, I like reading, or you built this deck with your sister, you’re kind of doing it day by day — at what point did you decide, “OK, this is a business now,” or, “This is how I’m gonna make my money”?**

Honestly, immediately, because I was a full-time model before. So my brand, aka Instagram, social media, who I am as a person, my haircuts, my skin — it's all my business. Because literally, if I didn’t show up as my best self to an audition, a self-tape, a casting, I was not gonna be able to pay rent at one point in my life, right?

So it was immediate, because I’ve always been, since 2023, well, 2018 technically, my brand. That’s why I read so many books: to get better at auditions and castings and to make sure I talk to every single person in the room, remember their names, et cetera. So yeah, honestly, immediately.

**What metrics actually matter to you now? Because I’ve talked to a lot of creators where they’re like, you know, it’s not so much about the views anymore. It’s really about the comments, the engagement. So what are you looking at?**

Yeah, that’s a great question because it’s easy to get caught up. Honestly, how my brain thinks, I’ll post one thing, and it doesn’t hit, and I'm like, “OK, it’s over. GGs. We fell off, it's wrapping up.” And then I’ll post something the next day, and it'll go crazy, and I’m like, “OK, I’m good.”

So I kind of took away from the likes and the views because I’m an overthinker sometimes. It’ll stop me in the way of, like, I want to post this, but it might not hit. And when I get in that mindset, I have to post it.

Because, for example, I had no idea the Spurs content would be among my best-performing content. I had no idea, because I'm like, my demographic really hasn’t shown any love for sports. And then the World Cup and Spurs content went insane. I was like, that’s so dope that I can share another part of my life with people.

But to answer your question, comments for sure. I love the comments because it shows that people care. I kind of care, and it's cool just to talk to them and like the comment. Everything else comes and goes, so yeah, I kind of just focus on the feedback I get.

**What is something that, if someone was gonna start creating content tomorrow, you would advise them to do?**

Choose pieces to make content about that you can do a lot with, in the sense of...don’t do what's popular right off the bat. Yeah, doing the trends is fun, and it’s awesome. People love seeing their favorite creators do trends. But you need to have specific things. Not even necessarily a niche, but just a few things that you can make content about where you don’t get tired.

If you don’t like something but you make content about it, you’re gonna get exhausted. If I hated books and I had to do a book review, I’d be sick to my core. So, as cliché as it sounds, I would genuinely make content about things that you love.

**And finally, I know mental health and your journey have been a really big part of your content, like you said. That’s a level of vulnerability that some creators don’t cross. So why did you decide that you were going to be open about reading the self-improvement books, things like that, your mental health? You even mentioned going to therapy right after leaving the villa, which is so important, by the way, and not a lot of people talk about it. Why was that something that you wanted to share?**

That’s a great question. I think at first it was because I got so many questions about, "How did you handle yourself in the villa so well?” Or, “How did you not crash out?” And it was really because I’ve been in therapy for three years in October, and then reading self-mastery books since 2020.

So I just shared because people expect you to be the nonchalant, good-looking guy. It's just like, bro, I am who I am. And you have to be genuine in this world, or people will — I just feel like it’s so weird to pretend to be something you’re not or be fake or put on the mask.

This is me. Yes, obviously not everything should be shared, but people are asking me, "How did you not crash out?" It’s like, no, I love therapy. My hot take on every single questionnaire I get is that everyone should be in therapy and read books.

Because I promise, if someone reads three self-mastery books, like *The Four Agreements*, *When Things Fall Apart*, and *The Subtle Art of Not Giving a F\*ck*, they would be unrecognizable. You’d actually be unrecognizable in three months.

And so I think I’m just so passionate about it because it changed my life and it gave me a second life, so to speak. Genuinely, it gave me another life.

And now I get to do this, and I’m so blessed. So why would I ever want to gatekeep that? And I think it’s so cool to be vulnerable and show, especially young guys — obviously I love my audience, but young guys — like, yo, it’s OK to cry, it’s OK to be vulnerable, it’s OK to be called soft. Because it’s like, bro, it just is.

entries.title: Dell Stock Surges On Record Orders For AI Servers
entries.content:
Dell reported record fiscal Q2 results as AI server demand surged, booking $60.9 billion in AI server orders and ending the quarter with a $95 billion backlog. From a report: The company posted record revenue of $47 billion, up 58% year over year. Earnings per share came in at $6.34, up 273% from a year ago. Adjusted earnings rose 203% to $7.04 per share.
"With AI momentum accelerating and our opportunity expanding across the portfolio, we're raising our full-year FY27 revenue outlook by $25 billion to $192 billion, up nearly 70% year over year," said Jeff Clarke, CEO of Dell Technologies, in the company's earnings release.
Dell has seen its orders balloon as enterprise customers adopt artificial intelligence and use AI servers locally to run agentic AI queries. Dell stock is up more than 230% year to date. Peer Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE), which also moved up 110% since the start of the year, jumped in after-hours trading.

entries.title: TeamCity 2026.2: Pipelines General Availability, BYOK for AI Assistant, and More
entries.content:
This major update for TeamCity On-Premises introduces a number of pipeline improvements that are now moving out of EAP and joining build configurations as official, stable options for designing CI/CD workflows. We are also shipping a number of AI-related features, including an MCP toolset extension and the ability to choose any major cloud AI provider or your local LLM to handle all interactions with AI Assistant in TeamCity. As always, you can see the complete list in [our documentation](https://www.jetbrains.com/help/teamcity/2026.2/what-s-new-in-teamcity.html).

We also roll out two bug-fix updates for our previous major TeamCity On-Premises versions: [2025.11.8](https://www.jetbrains.com/help/teamcity/2025.11/teamcity-2025-11-8-release-notes.html) and [2026.1.4](https://www.jetbrains.com/help/teamcity/2026.1/teamcity-2026-1-4-release-notes.html).

## TeamCity pipelines

### General availability

TeamCity 2025.07 introduced pipelines as an Early Access Program (EAP) feature – instantly available on TeamCity Cloud and on request for TeamCity On-Premises. Since then, we’ve been steadily closing the gap with classic build configurations, adding build feature support, .NET steps, the ability to link pipelines into build chains, and more.

With this release, pipelines move out of EAP and are now generally available on both TeamCity Cloud and On-Premises, for projects of any size and complexity.

However, our development of pipelines does not stop here – see our [roadmap](https://www.jetbrains.com/help/teamcity/pipelines-roadmap.html) for what’s next.

### Improved branch handling

Pipelines are now much better equipped to handle branches when your YAML file is stored in a Git repository. You can now select repository branches while in *Edit* mode, and design unique workflows for each branch.

![](https://blog.jetbrains.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/pipelines-edit-mode-branch-selector.png)

In addition, pipelines are now better at handling protected branches – the most common technique for safeguarding your main branches from unverified commits. Starting with version 2026.2, pipelines show clear warnings that edits made in the UI cannot be pushed to protected branches directly, and suggest saving them to other branches instead.

Learn more: [Feature branches](https://www.jetbrains.com/help/teamcity/2026.2/pipeline-settings.html#Feature+Branches)

### Run through failures﻿

When setting up job dependencies, you can now enable *Run job even if upstream fails* to ensure a pipeline runs until the very end, even when there are errors.

![](https://blog.jetbrains.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/run-if-upstream-fails.png)

The pipeline run will still be marked as failed overall, but this feature lets you ensure  that specific jobs (for example, cleanup or notification steps) always run.

Learn more: [Job dependencies](https://www.jetbrains.com/help/teamcity/2026.2/job-settings.html#Dependencies)

### Promote pipeline runs

*Promote* – the button that triggers the downstream part of a build chain from an older, already finished build – now works for pipelines, not just build configurations.

![](https://blog.jetbrains.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/promote-pipeline-run.png)

For example, you can promote a successful *Build Docker image* run into the *Upload to DockerHub* configuration or pipeline to re-deploy that artifact without rebuilding it.

Learn more: [Partial chain execution](https://www.jetbrains.com/help/teamcity/2026.2/run-build-chains.html#Partial+chain+execution)

### Debug jobs

You can now debug individual jobs without leaving *Edit* mode and triggering the entire pipeline. This small addition allows you to design complex workflows faster because you can fix problems as they arise instead of having to work your way through the failure log at the very end.

![](https://blog.jetbrains.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/debug-jobs.png)

Learn more: [Debug jobs](https://www.jetbrains.com/help/teamcity/2026.2/create-and-edit-pipelines.html#Debug+Jobs)

### Unbound pipelines

You can now create pipelines without VCS roots attached. Previously, this option was only available for build configurations. Choose the *Without repository* option when creating a pipeline to create a custom workflow that does not check out any remote sources.

![](https://blog.jetbrains.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/pipeline-without-repo.png)

Learn more: [Create and edit pipelines](https://www.jetbrains.com/help/teamcity/create-and-edit-pipelines.html)

### New MCP tools

Your AI Agents can now use three more tools designed to work with TeamCity pipelines: `teamcity_pipeline_get`, `teamcity_pipeline_post`, and `teamcity_pipeline_delete`. To avoid any accidents, the `post` and `delete` tools are only available in [Brave mode](https://www.jetbrains.com/help/teamcity/2026.2/ai-agent-integration.html#Safety+Concerns), which has to be enabled manually.

Learn more: [TeamCity MCP](https://www.jetbrains.com/help/teamcity/2026.2/ai-agent-integration.html#TeamCity+MCP)

## TeamCity AI

AI continues to reshape software development. The TeamCity team is taking a practical approach: using AI to solve real CI/CD problems and remove friction from everyday tasks – all while keeping you in control of which AI capabilities you use and how you use them.

### AI Assistant

AI Assistant now supports Bring Your Own Key (BYOK), enabling you to plug in any supported LLM. Go to *Admin | AI Assistant* and enter your developer AI API key. Then you’ll be able to use Anthropic, OpenAI, Google Gemini, or any other supported model to inspect the builds and debug your CI workflows.

![](https://blog.jetbrains.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/aia-anthropic.png)

Learn more: [AI providers](https://www.jetbrains.com/help/teamcity/2026.2/ai-assistant.html#Providers)

### MCP enhancements

In version 2026.1, we have implemented an MCP endpoint that allows AI agents to use a TeamCity server as a source of tools. In this release, we’re adding three more tools that let you use your preferred AI solutions to manage pipelines in addition to classic build configurations and projects.

Moreover, we have implemented the OAuth/PKCE authorization flow, which means you no longer need to manually issue a personal access token and pass it to your AI environment configuration.

Learn more: [TeamCity MCP](https://www.jetbrains.com/help/teamcity/2026.2/ai-agent-integration.html#TeamCity+MCP)

## Rerun failed chain builds

The *Dependencies* tab of build configuration settings now includes a *Retry Settings* group.

![](https://blog.jetbrains.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/image-72.png)

Enable the *Use custom retry settings* option and enter a positive number of retry attempts in the corresponding box when you want to delay a downstream build and automatically retry a failing dependency in place – no need to rerun the entire chain.

Learn more: [Dependency retry settings](https://www.jetbrains.com/help/teamcity/2026.2/configuring-dependencies.html#Dependency+retry+settings)

## IDE integrations

We’ve updated our [IDEA plugin](https://plugins.jetbrains.com/plugin/25142-teamcity-experimental-) so that it now comes with our [CLI tool](https://www.jetbrains.com/help/teamcity/teamcity-cli.html) and offers seamless MCP server registration. This means you can set up integration with Junie or third-party AI agents with little to no manual setup.

The plugin core functionality has also been improved: You can now view the results of TeamCity tests from the IDE and launch remote runs with local changes that have not yet been committed.

In addition, [Kotlin Multiplatform](https://kotlinlang.org/docs/multiplatform/get-started.html) developers working with IDEA and Android Studio can now install this plugin to claim an exclusive free-tier TeamCity Cloud subscription (currently capped at 30,000 build credits per month) where it’s possible to run automatically generated pipelines that test and build your iOS applications. The plugin also simplifies TestFlight integration, making the process of deploying your iOS applications significantly easier.

## GitHub﻿ integration

The *Pull Requests* build feature can now match pull requests by their source branch instead of their branch reference. This lets TeamCity recognize separate pull requests in different repositories as related changes and build them together in the same build chain, even when GitHub assigns them different pull request numbers.

Learn more: [GitHub pull requests](https://www.jetbrains.com/help/teamcity/2026.2/pull-requests.html#GitHub+Pull+Requests)

## DSL compilation mode

For projects that store Kotlin DSL versioned settings in remote repositories, you can now choose where TeamCity runs this code: [on the server or build agents](https://www.jetbrains.com/help/teamcity/2026.2/kotlin-dsl.html#DSL+Compilation).

![](https://blog.jetbrains.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/image-73.png)

Executing kDSL on build agents is less restricting and more secure, but both options come with certain trade-offs, so make sure to check our documentation for all recommendations and caveats.

entries.title: The MPS 2026.2 Early Access Program Has Started
entries.content:
MPS 2026.2 EAP1 offers several improvements to test reporting, enhances grouping of found items, and brings a smoother editing experience and a more maintainable foundation for launching MPS and MPS-based products. This release makes multi-node selection more predictable and aligns the MPS startup configuration more closely with the IntelliJ Platform.

[DOWNLOAD MPS 2026.2 EAP1](https://www.jetbrains.com/mps/nextversion/)

Along with numerous bug fixes, this build introduces several key improvements.

## Editor tests: Flexible result matching

When an editor test does not need to match the expected result exactly – for example, when the order of child nodes or the value of an attribute is irrelevant – you can now tell MPS which differences to ignore.

There are two ways to customize result matching:

* **Node-matching rules:** Declare custom matching rules. You can specify which containment roles should be compared, ignored, or excluded, and which properties or references should not be compared.
* **Per-node markers:** When the exception applies to just one node, add a marker directly to that node in the result fixture using the intentions menu.

![Editor tests flexible result matching](https://blog.jetbrains.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/MarkIgnored_2.png)

Either way, the parts you don’t care about stop causing false failures – and when a test does fail, the message now points straight at the node and cell responsible, so there’s no more sleuthing through raw assertions.

This improvement is the result of a direct customer request. It ensures fewer brittle editor tests and less fixture babysitting.

## More informative test failure messages

Editor test failures – a wrong selection, a mismatched editor cell “ID”, or a wrong selection range – now describe exactly which node and cell are involved instead of reporting a bare assertion failure. Every node mentioned in a failure message is rendered along with its presentation, concept name, and node ID, making it much easier to locate the problematic node in the result fixture without reproducing the failure in the debugger.

![More informative editor test failure messages](https://blog.jetbrains.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/TestFailureMsgs_1.png)

## Virtual packages in *Find Usages* results

The *Find Usages* results tree now supports grouping by virtual package. When it’s enabled, usage results are nested under folder nodes corresponding to the virtual package of each root node, mirroring the structure shown in the *Project* pane. This makes it easier to locate root nodes in large models with many virtual folders.

Dotted virtual package names, for example `com.example.ui`, expand into one tree level per segment, so the nesting in *Find Usages* matches the nested virtual folders in the *Project* view.

The new *Group by virtual package* toggle appears on the *Find Usages* toolbar, alongside the existing grouping options, such as module, model, and root node. It is enabled by default for *Find Usages*. Other tool windows that display usage results – *Model Checker*, *TODO*, *Dependencies Viewer*, and *Refactoring View* – retain their usual default grouping options.

![Group by virtual package toggle in Find Usages results](https://blog.jetbrains.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/FindUsagesVirtualPackage_1.png)

## A more natural way to select lists of nodes

Selecting a larger piece of a model in the MPS editor is now easier with *Select Up* (*Ctrl+Up*). When the caret is inside a list of nodes – for example, a sequence of statements in a behavior method or a constraint – *Select Up* now recognizes the list as a meaningful editing unit.

Instead of jumping directly from one node to its parent, the action first selects all sibling nodes in the list. The parent is selected in the following step. This gives the selection process an intuitive intermediate level and makes common operations, such as copying and pasting a complete group of statements, faster and more reliable.

This also works correctly when the current selection is already a range of nodes, so repeated *Select Up* actions provide a consistent path from an individual node, through its containing list, to the surrounding structure.

## Startup configuration aligned with the IntelliJ Platform

MPS 2026.2 updates the way startup scripts and product metadata are assembled. The MPS build tooling now keeps the platform-provided boot classpath separate from the MPS-specific extension classpath. It also exposes additional JVM arguments as part of the MPS startup script configuration.

This separation allows MPS distributions to consume the boot classpath and JVM options defined by the matching IntelliJ Platform build, while adding only the libraries and settings specific to MPS. Platform updates can therefore be integrated with less manual maintenance and a lower risk of stale launcher configuration.

The generated launchers also apply platform access options more precisely. Shared `--add-opens` options come from the platform metadata, while operating-system-specific packages are added only to the launcher for the corresponding operating system. This keeps the launch configuration consistent across macOS, Linux, and Windows and helps prevent startup problems caused by outdated or unnecessarily broad JVM arguments.

Together, these changes make the MPS launcher more resilient as the underlying platform evolves and provide a cleaner extension point for teams building custom MPS-based distributions.

You can review the complete list of fixed issues [here](https://youtrack.jetbrains.com/issues/MPS?q=state:Resolved%20version:%20%7B2026.2%20EAP1%7D%20%20order%20by:%20Priority%20%20).

Your JetBrains MPS team

entries.title: Stop Guessing at Hard Faults
entries.content:
**CLion’s new AI skill lets agents find the root cause without manual digging.**

Embedded debugging takes a lot of manual work. You’re flashing real hardware, juggling debug probes or DAP adapters, and when something goes wrong at a lower level (a hard fault), the processor doesn’t tell you why, only that it happened. Finding the actual cause means manually decoding CFSR and HFSR, cross-referencing the faulting program counter with disassembly, and often reproducing the crash several times to narrow it down.

[CLion 2026.2.2](https://www.jetbrains.com/clion/download/) now handles exactly this for you with a new AI skill for hard fault debugging, backed by dedicated MCP tooling. The agent reads the fault registers, inspects memory and disassembly, and traces the problem back to its source – using the same debugger tools you would, just without you having to drive each step by hand. The solution is vendor-agnostic and is compatible with any debugging tool, including Lauterbach TRACE32, Segger J-Link, and ST-LINK. It’s also available for any agent run in CLion with access to the IDE’s MCP server.

[](https://blog.jetbrains.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/hard_fault_claude.mp4)

#### Why does a hard fault tell you nothing?

A hard fault is an ARM Cortex-M CPU exception that occurs when something goes seriously wrong at a low level – for example, accessing invalid memory or overflowing the stack. The processor cannot safely continue running the code that triggered the fault. Developers can implement a handler that’s automatically called when a hard fault occurs. It typically captures forensic data before the state is lost, such as stacked registers and fault status registers. By default, though, most handlers halt execution without decoding the data, so they tell you only that a fault occurred, not the reason. That’s why debugging a hard fault can be difficult without additional tooling.

The hard fault skill is called *clion-embedded-hardfault* and is enabled by default in *Settings | Tools | AI Assistant | Skills | Bundled skills*. To use the skill, ensure you have enabled the MCP server in *Settings | Tools | MCP Server*.

## Why not just let an agent run shell commands and read the code?

An agent with shell and file access can already attempt this, running a debugger command, reading the output, and guessing what to do next. Without dedicated tooling, that’s roughly what a hard fault investigation looks like – slow, and dependent on the agent correctly parsing register dumps from raw text.

The *clion-embedded-hardfault* skill activates on a narrower, well-defined trigger: a session stopped in `HardFault_Handler` (or its siblings `MemManage_Handler`, `BusFault_Handler`, `UsageFault_Handler`), or a mention of CFSR, HFSR, MMFAR, BFAR, or an exception stack frame. Instead of handing the agent a raw register dump to parse from text, it hands over evidence that’s already decoded. The fault status registers are interpreted rather than dumped. The hardware-stacked exception frame is captured before it can be overwritten. And the SVD-decoded peripheral registers behind the faulting memory-mapped access arrive alongside the disassembly and memory around the faulting instruction.

That data comes from CLion’s own understanding of memory maps, registers, and instruction encoding – not reconstructed by parsing terminal output. The agent starts from the actual faulting address and its meaning, instead of working backward from a crash log or staring at an infinite loop in a Cortex-M startup file.

## How to debug a hard fault with an agent

When a debug session stops in a hard fault handler, run your preferred agent in CLion’s AI chat or terminal. Describe the problem in natural language, for example: *“sometimes this hard faults, prob invalid mem access, find issue, make no mistakes”*. You can also name the skill explicitly to make the task clearer.

The agent will follow the skill instructions to use the appropriate IDE tools via MCP.

![](https://blog.jetbrains.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/hard_fault_claude_1_small.png)

When the agent identifies the cause of the hard fault, it provides a detailed description, including where the bug is located and how to fix it.

![](https://blog.jetbrains.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/hard_fault_claude_2_small.png)

You can fix the bug manually or ask the agent to do this for you, including re-running the debug session to verify that the program works as expected.

## Limitations

The hard fault debugging skill works in both AI chat and CLI mode for Claude Code and Codex, but only in CLI mode for GitHub Copilot.

## Other debugger tools available for agents

The hard fault debugging skill is the next step in our improvements to [agentic debugging](https://blog.jetbrains.com/clion/2026/07/2026-2-release/#debugger-skill-for-ai-agents). The underlying MCP tooling, though, is helpful for debugging embedded projects in general, giving agents access to memory, register values, and disassembly. These are useful for debugging non-embedded C and C++ projects, too.

In addition to the above, agents can perform [basic debugger actions](https://www.jetbrains.com/help/clion/agentic-debugging.html#capabilities):

* Start, pause, and stop a debug session.
* Set and remove breakpoints.
* Step through code.
* Read local variables, frame values, and nested fields.

You can find all the MCP tools available for your agents in *Settings | MCP Server | Exposed Tools*.

## Try the skill in CLion 2026.2.2

The AI skill for hard fault debugging is available in CLion 2026.2.2. It will also be added to the first upcoming [2026.3 EAP release](https://www.jetbrains.com/clion/nextversion/). Try the skill with your own Cortex-M MCU and let us know what would make the workflow better for you!

[DOWNLOAD CLION](https://www.jetbrains.com/clion/download/)
